title: Keane
full_review:
The days when English actors could barely manage credible American accents -- except perhaps for a Southern drawl -- are long past.

A spectacular case in point is Damian Lewis, so good as Soames in the recent PBS "The Forsyte Saga," giving an utterly convincing portrait of a schizophrenic, frantically pacing New York's Port Authority bus terminal in "Keane" (Magnolia).

Mumbling and sometimes violent, William Keane stops passers-by and boards buses looking for the daughter he claims was abducted. When not searching, he snorts cocaine, and has a rough sexual encounter with a woman he picks up at a bar (Tina Holmes, who played Maggie on "Six Feet Under"). The two are fully clothed, but the act is graphic nonetheless.

Just when you think his character is so base he's not worth the audience's trouble, Keane overhears a mother, Lynn (Amy Ryan), with 7-year-old daughter Kira (Abigail Breslin) in tow, having trouble paying her rent at the transient motel at which they're staying, and he selflessly offers to give her money.

This kind deed leads Lynn to ask Keane to share a takeout dinner in her room, and the experience brings out his essential goodness.

Lynn knows nothing of Keane's problems, and allows him to take care of her daughter when she abruptly -- and without forewarning -- leaves town to meet with her absent husband, who's taken a job in Albany.

Suddenly, you're on the edge of your seat wondering what the clearly unbalanced Keane may do if he's alone with the young and trusting child, but what transpires is not what you fear.

Writer-director Lodge Kerrigan's cinema-verite work -- which has been making the rounds of film festivals -- has an ugly milieu and several sordid situations. Furthermore, the first half is contrived and tedious, though the ending is intensely moving and redemptive.

Lewis is extraordinary, and there is first-class support by Ryan (Broadway's recent Stella in "A Streetcar Named Desire"), Breslin (an amazingly natural child performance) and, in her brief scene, Holmes.

This is a difficult and flawed film, and not for everyone, but those who stick with it will be keenly rewarded.

The film contains profanity and rough language, a violent episode, an unrestrained sexual encounter, and alcohol and drug use. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
